title: Focaccia
subtitle: an olive oil-rich Italian flatbread with a dimpled top
excerpt: Focaccia is one of the most forgiving yeasted breads to bake at home. The dough is wet and sticky, which is correct -- do not add more flour. A generous pour of olive oil gives it a crisp, golden underside and a soft, pillowy inside.
sourceNotes: Liguria, northern Italy. Focaccia al rosmarino is the classic version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze once fully cooled. Warm in a hot oven for 5 minutes to refresh.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prove in the tin overnight in the fridge. Add oil and dimple just before baking.

content.text: The trick to great focaccia is not skimping on the olive oil. It pools in the dimples and fries the base as the bread bakes. Use a good extra-virgin oil -- you will taste it. Rosemary is classic, but the topping can go in many directions.

items.prepNote: strong white bread flour if available

content.text: Mix the yeast and honey into the warm water. Leave for 5 minutes until foamy. Combine with the flour and salt to form a shaggy dough.
Pour 2 tablespoons of olive oil into a large bowl. Add the dough. Cover and leave for 1 hour until doubled.

Pour 3 tablespoons of olive oil into a deep roasting tin (roughly 30 x 20cm). Stretch the dough to fill the tin. It will spring back -- let it rest 10 minutes, then stretch again. Cover and prove for 45 minutes.
Heat the oven to 220C. Drizzle 2 more tablespoons of olive oil over the dough. Press your fingertips firmly into the surface to create deep dimples all over.
Scatter with fresh rosemary sprigs and flaky salt. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until golden brown on top and the underside is crisp. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes before cutting.

items.symptom: Focaccia is dry and bready rather than rich
items.fix: Be generous with the oil at every stage -- in the proving bowl, in the tin, and drizzled on top before baking.

items.symptom: Dough springs back and will not stay in the tin
items.cause: Gluten is tight. Dough needs more rest.
items.fix: Leave the dough to relax for 10 minutes between each stretch. Do not force it.

content.text: Focaccia comes from Liguria on the Italian Riviera, where it is eaten at all hours -- for breakfast, as a snack, alongside soup, or as a base for sandwiches. Bakeries in Genoa sell it warm by the slice from early morning. The version with rosemary and salt is the one most people know, but the format is endlessly adaptable.
